title: Prompt Cardinality Wrangler Lab
body:
Goal:
Quick, messy working notes on how the number and composition of few-shot exemplars (cardinality) interacts with: model size/quantization, token budgets, and redundancy in examples. Want to produce reproducible heuristics and a short checklist to include in prompt-library templates.

High-level hypotheses (for validation):
- Small models + quantized weights will prefer fewer, high-quality exemplars; extra tokens hurt more than they help due to context truncation and tokenization mismatches.
- Large models (>=70B) tolerate higher cardinality but benefit more from diverse negative examples (contrastive few-shot).
- Ordering matters: group by intent (positive pairs), then contrastive negatives last — avoids early anchor collapse.
- Repetition/homogeny among exemplars creates brittle overfitting to phrasing; diversity beats count when working with variable user phrasing.

Experiment matrix (quick):
- Models: rw-small-13b-pt, rw-medium-34b-q4, rw-large-70b, rw-xlarge-176b (use vernacular names used in infra).
- Cardinalities: 0,1,3,5,8,12 (and a long-ordered set truncated to token limit).
- Variants: identical-exemplar-phrasing, paraphrase-sampled, mixed-domain, contrastive-negative-included.
- Metrics: exact-match (for structured outputs), BLEU-ish (for short answers), hallucination rate (manual label), token-cost per effective-correct answer, median latency.

Quick test harness notes: (notes to self)
- Reuse the prompt-runner in /experiments/cardinality-runner; add args: --exemplar-count, --shuffle-variant (none|paraphrase|grouped).
- Record prefix cache hit rates (redwood runtime: KV cache) and batching sizes — these correlate with latency and cost; sometimes higher cardinality causes larger batch shapes and increases latency.
- Use a fixed seed for paraphrase generator (to reduce noise across runs).

Few-shot templates (sketch) — these are raw, intended for iteration:

Template A: Instruction-first + exemplars
Instruction: You are a concise assistant returning JSON with keys: {answer, rationale}. Keep answer <= 30 tokens.

Example 1:
User: "How many grams in a cup of flour?"
Assistant: {"answer":"120g","rationale":"Common cooking conversion: 1 cup all-purpose flour ≈ 120g"}

Example 2:
User: "Convert 2 cups sugar to grams"
Assistant: {"answer":"400g","rationale":"1 cup sugar ≈ 200g"}

Prompt (end):
User: "How many grams in 3/4 cup of flour?"
Assistant:

Template B: Role-first + contrastive negatives
Role: You are a careful unit converter. If ambiguous, ask for clarification.

Pos Example:
Q: "1 tbsp salt to grams"
A: {"answer":"18g","rationale":"1 tbsp salt ~ 18g depending on grain, assume table salt"}

Neg Example: (explicitly labelled bad)
Q: "1 cup sugar to grams"
A: (BAD) {"answer":"128g","rationale":"wrong conversion used for flour"}

Note: tag negatives clearly with a prefix 'BAD' so the model has contrastive signal. Anecdotal: some models learn to mimic the 'BAD' label and require additional negation instructions — watch for this.

Failure cases observed so far (field notes):
- Overfitting to syntax: when exemplars all end with punctuation style (e.g., question mark), the model sometimes echoes punctuation patterns into the JSON fields (nasty when expecting strict machine-parsable JSON).
- Early anchor trap: first exemplar strongly biases format; models replicate first example's minor idiosyncrasies when cardinality > 3.
- Negative labeling pitfalls: naive 'BAD' examples can backfire with small models that latch onto the label, producing more BAD-like answers; mitigations: add clarifying positive example after each negative, or use 'Example (incorrect): ... Fix:' pattern.
- Token-cost regressions: adding exemplars increased per-request tokens by 4–8x in some runs because we concatenated long user-system context; need to compute effective tokens per exemplar and cap at ~40 tokens for cheap models.

Observational snippets (raw):
- "34b-q4 dropped to 72% EM with 8 near-duplicate exemplars; 3 paraphrases got it to 86%."
- "70b improved with 5 examples placed in decreasing complexity order (simple->complex)."
- "Small model hallucinated units when exemplar used shorthand (g vs grams) — be explicit."

Checklist for creating exemplar sets (working):
- Limit tokens per exemplar: aim <40 tokens; truncate examples to keep structural cues but remove fluff.
- Diversity: at least 60% lexical/paraphrase variation; at least one negative where appropriate.
- Pacing: place the clearest, simplest exemplar first; follow with increasing complexity.
- Labeling: avoid binary 'BAD' tags unless model size >= medium; instead use 'Incorrect example — why wrong:' plus corrected form.
- Token-budget mode: include a 'budget-aware' variant that drops low-signal exemplars dynamically when user prompt + exemplar tokens > 1024.

Open questions / things to test next:
- Does interleaving negative examples between positives reduce anchor effects more than appending negatives?
- For structured outputs, is it better to show 1 long full example or 3 compact partial examples that cover edges? My hypothesis: partial coverage wins for edge-case robustness.
- Explore automated exemplar curation: cluster candidate few-shot examples by embedding distance, then greedily pick to maximize centroid coverage under token budget. Does that beat hand-curated sets?

Mini playbook: when writing a new prompt template for the library
1) Start with a single positive exemplar + instruction. Run on target models.
2) Add 2 paraphrases of the positive; check delta. If >5% EM improvement on target model, keep them.
3) Add 1 explicit negative (labelled with error + correction). If small model performance drops, remove and instead add a corrected positive.
4) If token budget exceeded, run budget-aware selector (pick top-K exemplars by similarity to query).

Quick logs and notes to self: 
- Save top-performing exemplar sets to /shared/experiments/cardinality/store with name pattern cardinality-<model>-<variant>-v1 (ask infra team for write perms).
- Sync with Maya on 2024-11-22 for cluster scheduling — she has a batch window to run the 8-model sweep.
- Link to JIRA: JIRA-FF-4623 contains baseline evals and scoring harness.

Next steps (actionable):
- Implement budget-aware exemplar selector in prompt-runner (2d).
- Run small-model ablation for 0,1,3,5 exemplars and collect token-cost curve (1 week).
- Draft short library guidance (1 A4 page) for prompt-library: trimmed checklist above.

Rough signature:
